strengths: Extends the recent CCDB method from a single-Gaussian, class-level distribution matching to a more expressive group-level mixture formulation, which is a reasonable and interpretable improvement.
The proposed FG-CCDB computes sample weights in closed form without any optimization, making it computationally lightweight and easy to integrate.

Extensive experiments across five diverse benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, cCIFAR10) show consistent gains over CCDB and competitive or superior performance relative to bias-supervised methods, especially in challenging multi-class, highly biased settings.

Good diagnostic analyses: correlation shift plots (Fig. 3), sample weight distributions (Fig. 5), and group-prediction-accuracy-vs-repetition curves (Fig. 4) provide some mechanistic insight into why the method works.
Ablation study (Table 3) meaningfully isolates the contributions of BEO and FG-CCDB by combining each with alternative supervised/unsupervised counterparts.
The bias exploration module (BEO) is shown to serve as a plausible substitute for human bias annotations when plugged into existing bias-supervised methods (GroupDRO-BEO, DFR-BEO).
weaknesses: Method fundamentally requires |Y| = |S| (one bias attribute per class), an assumption explicitly acknowledged as violated by CelebA and CivilComments in the conclusion; this restricts general applicability and the paper does not present a principled way to relax it.

The core novelty is somewhat incremental: BEO largely follows the “overfit-then-select-hard-samples” paradigm used by prior work (JTT, SELF, LfF, DFR), with the main differences being an extremely small initial split (γ=10%) and iterative top-50% confidence filtering, which are heuristic choices without strong theoretical justification.

No direct comparison of FG-CCDB's group-partitioning approach against alternative unsupervised group-discovery baselines (e.g., GMM/clustering-based fine-grained CCDB variants, GEORGE-style clustering) to isolate whether gains stem from finer distribution modeling per se or from the specific BEO procedure.

Writing quality has multiple grammatical errors and typos throughout (e.g., “foucus,” “banchmark,” “asses,” “bia-supervised,” “an novel”), which detracts from clarity and suggests limited proofreading.

Reporting inconsistencies: some baseline numbers in Tables 1–2 lack standard deviations (as they are taken from original papers), making direct statistical comparison to the proposed method less rigorous.

The gap between FG-CCDB and its fully supervised counterpart (FG-CCDB-sup) is often small, which is presented as a strength, but this also raises the question of how much added value the more complex BEO machinery provides beyond simpler group-detection heuristics.

No theoretical analysis or convergence guarantee is given for the iterative bias enhancement learning process; its effectiveness is demonstrated only empirically, and the number of repetitions (up to 3) is chosen empirically per dataset without deeper analysis of failure cases beyond the qualitative discussion in the conclusion.

strengths: The paper conducts fairly extensive experiments across five benchmark datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, cCIFAR10), covering both binary and challenging multi-class/highly-biased settings.
The proposed FG-CCDB reweighting scheme is computationally cheap (closed-form, no iterative optimization, negligible storage overhead) compared to some baselines.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies are included (Table 3 substituting BEO/FG-CCDB with ground-truth annotations; Figure 3 correlation analysis; Figure 4 studying repetition of bias-enhancement learning) that attempt to isolate the contribution of each component.

Strong empirical gains are shown in extreme multi-class bias settings (e.g., cMNIST/cCIFAR10 at very low bias-conflicting ratios), which is a genuinely useful demonstration of robustness under severe imbalance.
weaknesses: The central technical claim — that FG-CCDB improves on CCDB's 'single Gaussian' approximation by modeling distributions as 'mixtures of latent groups' — is not actually realized in the method. The derivation (Eqs. 2-4) never fits any Gaussian or mixture density; it simply counts samples per (predicted bias, class) group and computes empirical frequencies. This is standard inverse-group-frequency reweighting dressed up in distribution-matching language, so the paper's framing overstates the technical novelty relative to CCDB and to well-known group-balancing/reweighting schemes (e.g., GroupDRO-style balancing).

The BEO bias-exploration procedure (train on a small random subset, then retrain on high-confidence/majority-aligned samples, optionally repeated) is a fairly straightforward combination of ideas already present in JTT, LfF, SELF, and uLA (overfitting-based identification of majority/minority groups). The incremental novelty over this prior work is limited and not clearly delineated.

The method assumes |Y| = |S| (each class is dominated by a single bias attribute), and the authors themselves acknowledge in the conclusion that this assumption is violated by CelebA (single minority group) and CivilComments (asymmetric group structure) — two of the three real-world benchmarks used for the main results. It is unclear how/why the method still performs well despite violating its own core assumption on these datasets, which undermines confidence in the theoretical justification and generality of the approach.

Results are internally inconsistent in ways that are not explained: e.g., FG-CCDB-sup (using ground-truth bias labels) underperforms the unsupervised FG-CCDB on Waterbirds i.i.d. accuracy (91.54 vs 92.50) and is only marginally better on WorstGroup — a supervised variant should not generally underperform its unsupervised counterpart, and no explanation or discussion is given for this counterintuitive result.

Improvements over the direct baseline CCDB are inconsistent across settings: on Waterbirds, FG-CCDB is essentially on par with or slightly below CCDB (92.50 vs 92.59 i.i.d., 90.56 vs 90.48 WorstGroup), while larger gains appear mainly on CelebA/CivilComments/multi-class. This weakens the claim of a universally 'more thorough removal of spurious correlations.'

Many baseline numbers appear to be copied directly from other papers rather than reproduced under a unified protocol (evidenced by missing std devs for several baselines, e.g., GroupDRO, LFF, JTT, ERM, MASKTUNE variants), which makes head-to-head comparisons less rigorous and reproducibility harder to verify.

No code release is mentioned, and while hyperparameters are given in the appendix, several implementation details (e.g., exact architecture/training details for the multi-stage retraining, sensitivity to number of BEO repetitions beyond the reported plateau) are not fully justified or ablated with statistical rigor.

The writing contains numerous typos and grammatical errors throughout (e.g., 'foucus', 'banchmark', 'muti-class', 'differ or conflicting correlations', 'bia-supervised'), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread, which detracts from overall polish expected at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Well-motivated technical contribution: replacing CCDB's single-Gaussian approximation with a group-level (mixture) description is a sensible and clearly explained extension that addresses a real limitation of the base method.

The BEO bias-exploration procedure (initial biased learning + bias-enhancement retraining) is simple, requires no extra annotations, and is shown to produce group predictions that closely track ground-truth minority/majority splits (Figure 4).

FG-CCDB's group-level reweighting is derived in closed form (no iterative optimization) and only requires storing a small C×C matrix, giving a lightweight, scalable alternative to sample-level reweighting.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five widely used benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, cCIFAR10) with multiple bias-conflicting ratios, and comparisons against both bias-supervised and bias-agnostic baselines.

Careful ablation isolating the contributions of BEO and FG-CCDB (via BEO substituted into GroupDRO/DFR, and ground-truth labels substituted into FG-CCDB) convincingly shows both components add value independently.

Additional diagnostic analyses (feature-correlation shift in Figure 3, sample-weight distributions in Appendix C) support the claimed mechanism of spurious-correlation removal rather than relying purely on end accuracy numbers.

Strong empirical results, particularly in extreme multi-class bias settings (cMNIST/cCIFAR10 at 0.5–5% bias-conflicting ratio), where the method clearly outperforms both supervised and unsupervised baselines.
weaknesses: The core contribution is an incremental extension of a very recent (2025, possibly concurrent) method, CCDB; the theoretical framing (mutual-information objective, Eq. 1) is directly inherited rather than newly derived, and the main technical novelty reduces to discretizing distributions via predicted group labels.

The method assumes |Y| = |S| (equal number of classes and bias attributes), which is a significant restriction; the paper itself acknowledges in the conclusion that this breaks down on datasets like CelebA and CivilComments where group structure is irregular, limiting general applicability.

The BEO overfitting-based bias-exploration strategy is conceptually similar to existing hard-example/early-stopping approaches (JTT, LfF, SELF, XRM); the multi-stage retraining refinement is a reasonable but fairly incremental extension of these ideas.
No empirical runtime/memory comparison is provided to substantiate the claimed computational efficiency advantages over CCDB and sample-level reweighting methods.

Sensitivity of FG-CCDB to the accuracy of BEO's bias predictions is not deeply analyzed beyond the ablation in Table 3; it is unclear how performance degrades as bias-prediction accuracy decreases in more complex or noisier group structures.

The paper lacks a discussion of failure cases beyond the brief limitation paragraph, and does not explore extending the method to settings where the number of latent bias groups differs from the number of classes.

Minor clarity/writing issues (typos such as 'foucus', 'bia-supervised', 'muti-class', 'finial') and some notational inconsistencies (e.g., mixed use of W in Eq.3-4 for both matrix and per-sample weight) slightly reduce readability.

No explicit discussion of broader ethical/fairness implications despite the paper's direct relevance to fairness-sensitive applications (e.g., CivilComments toxicity, medical diagnosis mentioned in the intro).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated extension of CCDB: replacing the single-Gaussian approximation with a discrete, confusion-matrix-based multi-modal representation is a sensible way to capture intra-class heterogeneity caused by multiple/hidden bias modes.

The proposed MST bias-discovery procedure (small-fraction initial training + confidence-based filtering + iterative bias amplification) is simple, computationally cheap (small epoch counts, subsets of data), and empirically effective at recovering minority-group structure without annotations.

Extensive experimental evaluation across a wide range of settings: binary classification (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments), multi-shortcut (UrbanCars, including BG-only/CoObj-only variants), and highly-biased multi-class synthetic benchmarks (cMNIST, cCIFAR10) with varying bias-conflicting ratios.

Strong and up-to-date baseline coverage, including very recent bias-agnostic and label-free methods (CCDB, GERNE, DDB, DaC, XRM, ExMap, uLA), plus bias-supervised upper bounds (GroupDRO, DFR), giving a comprehensive comparative picture.

Good ablation studies decoupling MST and FG-CCDB contributions (e.g., GroupDRO/DFR combined with MST-predicted labels, FG-CCDB with ground-truth labels), which convincingly shows each component's independent value.

Reasonable theoretical framing connecting the reweighting objective to mutual information minimization and covariate balance/Equal Opportunity Fairness, and closed-form, low-overhead sample weight computation (mode-level rather than sample-level).

Detailed hyperparameter analysis (γ, β) and sensitivity studies, plus additional appendix analyses (weight distributions, recall/F1 comparisons, repetition convergence, computational cost) that support the robustness and reproducibility of the claims.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: MST recombines established ideas (bias amplification via removing bias-conflicting samples, confidence-based hard-sample selection, overfitting-based pseudo-labeling from JTT/LfF/DaC/Lee et al.), and FG-CCDB is a fairly direct discretization of the existing CCDB objective onto confusion-matrix cells rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

The framework assumes |S| = |Y| (bias label space matches class label space) and represents mode structure as a C×C matrix; for genuinely multi-attribute or higher-cardinality latent bias structures (e.g., combinatorial biases as in UrbanCars) this is a coarse compression that may lose information, even though empirical results are still favorable.

The intra-mode homogeneity assumption (uniform sample weight within each confusion-matrix cell) is acknowledged as a heuristic approximation in the appendix rather than derived from theory, and finer sub-mode structure is left unaddressed, which could limit performance in datasets with more complex intra-mode variation.

Performance depends on hyperparameters γ (initial split ratio) and β (confidence selection ratio) that are tuned empirically based on assumptions about the bias-aligned ratio exceeding 50%; this assumption can fail (as acknowledged for CelebA and CivilComments) and the paper's own limitation section admits reduced effectiveness in such scenarios.

Method relies fundamentally on the standard assumption that ERM overfits preferentially to spurious/simpler features; while well-supported by prior literature, this remains an assumption without a formal guarantee, and cases with weak/absent overfitting signal (as noted in the conclusion) are not resolved, only flagged as future work.

Some real-world results (e.g., CelebA/CivilComments i.i.d. accuracy trade-offs, or cases where WGA exceeds the fully supervised upper bound) warrant more careful discussion regarding what is being optimized and whether over-aggressive reweighting could hurt majority-group performance in other settings not tested.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and well-motivated limitation of the prior CCDB method (single-Gaussian approximation of class-conditional/marginal distributions) and proposes a natural, well-explained fine-grained extension (FG-CCDB) using a discrete confusion-matrix-based representation.

The proposed sample-weight computation (Eq. 3-4) is closed-form, avoids iterative optimization, and scales with negligible memory/compute overhead compared to CCDB's sample-level reweighting, which is a genuine practical advantage.

Extensive experiments spanning binary (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments), multi-shortcut (UrbanCars), and multi-class/highly-biased synthetic (cMNIST, cCIFAR10) settings, with several bias-conflicting ratios, give a reasonably broad empirical picture.

Useful ablations isolate the contributions of MST (bias exploration) and FG-CCDB (distribution matching) independently by combining each with existing supervised/bias-agnostic baselines (e.g., GroupDRO-MST, FG-CCDB-sup), supporting the claim that both components contribute independently.

The paper reports hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (γ, β) and provides some justification (bias-aligned ratio argument) for default choices, plus additional rebuttal-stage experiments (adaptive β, additional repetitions, recall of minority groups) that strengthen the empirical support for design choices.
weaknesses: The core assumption that the bias label space S has the same cardinality as the class label space Y (|S|=|Y|) is a significant structural restriction; it ties the fine-grained description directly to a square confusion matrix and may not generalize to settings where the number of latent bias modes differs from the number of classes, or where biases are continuous/high-dimensional. This limitation is only acknowledged briefly (CelebA, CivilComments) rather than being rigorously analyzed.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the paper largely substitutes a single Gaussian in CCDB's KL-divergence objective with a discrete multi-modal (confusion-matrix-based) approximation; the MST bias-exploration procedure itself is an assembly of ideas already present in prior work (bias amplification via removing bias-conflicting samples, ERM overfitting as a bias signal, top-confidence filtering), without a fundamentally new mechanism.

Despite being framed as hyperparameter/annotation-free, MST still depends on two hand-tuned hyperparameters (γ for initial split size, β for high-confidence filtering, and the number of repetitions), whose default values are justified mainly via empirical sweet-spot arguments and dataset-specific bias-align ratios rather than a principled, data-driven selection procedure.

The theoretical justification connecting MST to the Equal Opportunity Fairness criterion (Appendix E) is informal/post-hoc rather than a rigorous analysis, and the core claim that ERM accuracy a<100% guarantees meaningful bias capture is not formally established beyond a toy illustrative example.

Performance trade-offs are not always favorable: in several tables (e.g., Waterbirds, CelebA i.i.d. accuracy in Table 1), FG-CCDB's in-distribution accuracy is sometimes lower than CCDB or other baselines even when WGA improves, and this trade-off is not thoroughly quantified or discussed.

Some recently proposed label-free baselines (DDB, GERNE, DaC, ExMap) are only compared on a subset of datasets/metrics rather than uniformly across all benchmarks, making some of the paper's comparative claims (e.g., 'significantly outperforms' in multi-class/multi-shortcut settings) harder to fully verify.

The assumption of intra-mode homogeneity (uniform sample weight within a mode) is acknowledged as a simplification; the authors' own experiments with entropy-based intra-mode splitting show degraded performance, suggesting the current coarse mode structure may still be insufficiently fine-grained in some cases, somewhat undercutting the 'fine-grained' framing of the contribution.
The paper's writing is dense and notation-heavy in places (e.g., Section 3.2), which could hinder reproducibility and clarity for readers not already deeply familiar with CCDB.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated limitation of prior work (CCDB's single-Gaussian approximation) and proposes a principled fine-grained extension (FG-CCDB) using a discrete confusion-matrix-based multi-modal distribution.

MST is a reasonably novel bias-exploration mechanism that systematically amplifies model overfitting through multi-stage data-selective retraining, and the paper provides intuitive and partially theoretical justification (connection to Equal Opportunity Fairness) for why this should work.

Extensive experimentation across a wide range of settings: single-shortcut binary classification (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments), multi-shortcut (UrbanCars), and highly-biased multi-class scenarios (cMNIST, cCIFAR10) with varying bias-conflicting ratios.

Strong empirical results—FG-CCDB matches or exceeds bias-supervised methods in several settings and significantly outperforms other bias-agnostic baselines, particularly in multi-class and multi-shortcut settings.

Good ablation studies isolating the contributions of MST and FG-CCDB independently (e.g., GroupDRO-MST, DFR-MST, FG-CCDB-sup), which convincingly demonstrate that both components contribute value on their own.
Thorough analysis of the quality of bias exploration (F1/precision/recall against ground truth) and hyperparameter sensitivity (γ, β), improving confidence in the robustness of the method.
Sample-weight computation is closed-form and lightweight, avoiding the storage/computation overhead of CCDB's per-sample Gaussian-based reweighting.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental relative to CCDB—the main idea is replacing a single Gaussian with a discrete confusion-matrix-based multi-modal representation, which, while effective, is a fairly natural extension rather than a conceptually new framework.

MST involves several heuristic design choices (γ=10%, β=50%, number of repetitions=3) that are tuned empirically per dataset property (e.g., bias-aligned ratio) rather than derived from a principled criterion; the adaptive-β variant is only briefly explored.

The mode definition assumes |S|=|Y| and relies on the hard confusion matrix, which inherently limits granularity to a C×C grid; the paper acknowledges (in appendix) that finer intra-mode substructure is not modeled, which could be limiting for datasets with complex, entangled biases beyond a single dominant shortcut per class.

The method's effectiveness is explicitly noted to degrade in scenarios where the overfitting signal fails to capture the bias (e.g., CelebA's single minority group, CivilComments' imbalanced class structure), suggesting the approach's applicability may be narrower than the broad claims in the abstract might imply.

Multiple moving parts (two-stage biased model training + confidence-based selective retraining + repeated bias enhancement + fine-grained reweighting) add complexity that could hinder reproducibility and practical adoption compared to simpler baselines.

Some benchmark results show FG-CCDB trading off i.i.d. accuracy versus WGA (e.g., ERM's much higher CelebA i.i.d. accuracy vs. FG-CCDB's lower i.i.d. but higher WGA), and the paper doesn't deeply analyze this trade-off or its implications for typical deployment scenarios where i.i.d. performance matters.
